lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Where should your eyes rest, and which edges should the contour follow, when you draw a chipped enamel mug before any shading?

FEEDBACK
Keep your eyes on the enamel mug, and draw the rim, the chip and the outer handle as edges you see, still with no shading. A chip is part of the contour if you can see it; do not smooth it away to make a perfect symbol. The line can be imperfect as long as it was made while looking.

WATCH FOR
A neat mug symbol drawn from memory, then shaded heavily, is a better first contour than a slow line made while looking.
lesson.independent_task:

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Sam draws one slow contour of a plain white kitchen mug and leaves every area unshaded. He starts where the handle meets the body, follows the outer rim as an ellipse, comes down the side, and returns along the handle. His pencil pauses whenever his eye pauses, so small changes in the rim stay in the line. The paper remains light because shading is a later lesson.

TRY FIRST
Where should your eyes rest, and which edges should the contour follow, when you draw a chipped enamel mug before any shading?

FEEDBACK
Keep your eyes on the enamel mug, and draw the rim, the chip and the outer handle as edges you see, still with no shading. A chip is part of the contour if you can see it; do not smooth it away to make a perfect symbol. The line can be imperfect as long as it was made while looking.

WHY IT MATTERS

visuals.alt: A slow contour follows the mug rim while the page stays unshaded.
visuals.teaches: Look longer at the mug than the paper, and draw the edge before any tone.

visuals.alt: The seen rim, side and handle compared with a remembered mug symbol.
visuals.teaches: The contour records edges in front of you, including dents and the handle join.
